You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Design a power interface for a piezoelectric energy harvester.
    *   Input: Sinusoidal current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25 nF) and $R_{leak}$ (20 M$\Omega$).
    *   Output: $V_{out}$ at node "out", powering $R_L$.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (min supply).
        *   $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (abs max).
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (ripple).
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (startup).
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (settled).
    *   Operating Conditions: S1 (nominal), S2 (heavy load), S3 (strong excitation/light load), S4 (weak excitation), S5 (low freq), S6 (hot/high $C_p$).
    *   Reference Design (FBR):
        *   S1: OK except settled (dv FAIL).
        *   S2: $V_{avg}$ FAIL (1.76V), $t_{up}$ FAIL.
        *   S3: $V_{max}$ FAIL (5.72V), ripple FAIL, settled FAIL.
        *   S4: $V_{avg}$ FAIL (1.51V), $t_{up}$ FAIL, settled FAIL.
        *   S5: settled FAIL.
        *   S6: OK.

    *   The FBR fails on low power (S4) and high power (S3).
    *   Low power (S4): $V_{avg}$ is too low. This suggests we need a more efficient way to extract energy than simple diode rectification, possibly using an inductor to step up voltage or recover charge.
    *   High power (S3): $V_{max}$ is too high. We need a way to clamp the voltage.
    *   Stability/Settling: $dv$ and $vpp$ constraints are tight. A large output capacitor is needed, but we must ensure it charges quickly enough ($t_{up}$).
    *   Efficiency: With $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{ V}$, diode drops (0.25V for DSCH) are significant.

    *   *Standard Rectifier (FBR):* Already tried. Too inefficient for S4, too unregulated for S3.
    *   *Synchronous Switching Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI):* Uses a switch and inductor to invert the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks, effectively increasing the extracted energy.
    *   *Parallel-SSHI:* A variation that might be more efficient.
    *   *Buck-Boost or Boost:* Harder with the given components (limited switches, no PWM controller, only SYNC).
    *   *Zener Clamp:* Necessary to prevent $V_{out} > 3.6\text{ V}$.

    *   **Topology 1: FBR with Zener Clamp.**
        *   Adding a Zener diode (DZ33) to the output of the FBR will solve the $V_{max}$ issue of S3.
        *   However, it doesn't help with the low power of S4 or the slow startup.

    *   **Topology 2: SSHI (Synchronous Switching Harvesting on Inductor).**
        *   The core idea: An inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ are used to flip the voltage across $C_p$ at the current peaks.
        *   Basic SSHI structure: Inductor $L$ connected to $pzp$, switch $S$ connected from the other end of $L$ to $pzn$. Rectifier from $pzp/pzn$ to $out$.
        *   Wait, the prompt provides `S` as a switch and `SYNC` as a controller.
        *   SSHI circuit:
            - $L$ between $pzp$ and $n1$.
            - $S$ between $n1$ and $pzn$.
            - Rectifier: $D_1$ ($pzp \to out$), $D_2$ ($pzn \to out$), $D_3$ ($0 \to pzp$), $D_4$ ($0 \to pzn$).
            - This allows flipping $C_p$ voltage.
            - Actually, a simpler SSHI often uses a half-bridge or specific diode arrangements. Let's try a standard SSHI-style interface.

    *   **Topology 3: SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction).**
        *   SECE is usually more efficient than SSHI.
        *   Structure: Inductor $L$ and switches. When $V_{pzp}$ hits a peak, a switch connects $C_p$ to $L$. Then $L$ transfers energy to $C_{out}$.
        *   Given the components (only 2 SYNCs, 4 switches), we can implement a simplified version.
        *   Let's consider a "buck-boost-like" synchronous converter.

    *   S2 (Heavy load) and S4 (Weak excitation) are the hardest for $V_{avg}$.
    *   S3 (Strong excitation) is the hardest for $V_{max}$.
    *   A Zener diode (DZ33) is essential for S3.
    *   To improve S2/S4, we need to extract more charge. SSHI is a good candidate.

    *   *Circuit A (FBR + Zener):* Basic, helps $V_{max}$, might still fail S2/S4.
    *   *Circuit B (SSHI + Zener):* Use an inductor and a switch to flip the capacitor voltage, followed by a bridge and a zener.
    *   *Circuit C (Simplified SECE/Charge Pump):* Use a switch to transfer charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$ via $L$.

    *   *Structure of SSHI proposed:*
        - Inductor $L1$: $[pzp, n1]$
        - Switch $S1$: $[n1, pzn]$
        - Controller $G1$: `edges: "both"`, `ton: pi*sqrt(L*Cp)`.
        - This flips the voltage across $C_p$.
        - Now we need to rectify this. The voltage at $pzp$ will now have larger swings.
        - Full bridge: $D_1 [pzp, out], D_2 [pzn, out], D_3 [0, pzp], D_4 [0, pzn]$.
        - Zener: $D_z [0, out]$.
        - Storage: $C_{out} [out, 0]$.

    *Wait*, is there a simpler way? The "reference design" was just a bridge. Let's try to improve it.
    What if we use a half-bridge if the piezo is symmetric? (It's a current source in parallel with $C_p$ and $R_{leak}$ between $pzp$ and $pzn$).
    Usually, we ground $pzn$ for a half-bridge. But the piezo is $pzp$ and $pzn$. Let's keep it floating and use a full bridge.

    *Alternative Structure (Half-bridge SSHI):*
    $pzn$ connected to $0$.
    $L1$ from $pzp$ to $n1$.
    $S1$ from $n1$ to $0$.
    $D1$ from $pzp$ to $out$.
    $D2$ from $0$ to $pzp$.
    $D_z$ from $0$ to $out$.
    Wait, this is only for half the cycle.

    Let's stick to:
    1.  **FBR + Zener** (Baseline improvement for S3).
    2.  **SSHI + FBR + Zener** (Voltage flipping to improve S2, S4).
    3.  **A different SSHI variation (e.g., using a switch to bypass diodes during flipping).**

    Let's refine the SSHI:
    - $L$ between $pzp$ and $n1$.
    - $S$ between $n1$ and $pzn$.
    - $G$ tracks peaks.
    - Bridge: $D_1[pzp, out], D_2[pzn, out], D_3[0, pzp], D_4[0, pzn]$.
    - $D_z[0, out]$.
    - $C_{out}[out, 0]$.

    *Wait*, the `ton` is very short ($1\mu\text{s}$ max). $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$ for $L=10\text{mH}, C_p=25\text{nF}$ is $\pi \sqrt{2.5 \times 10^{-7}} \approx 1.5\text{ms}$.
    The $t_{on}$ limit is $1\text{ms}$ ($0.001\text{s}$). So $L$ cannot be too large.
    $L = 1\text{mH} \implies \pi \sqrt{2.5 \times 10^{-8}} \approx 0.5\text{ms}$. That fits.

    Wait, if $t_{on}$ is limited to $1\text{ms}$, let's check if SSHI is feasible. Yes, $0.5\text{ms}$ is fine.

    *Wait, look at the Reference Design results again:*
    S2: $V_{avg} = 1.76\text{V}$. It's *very* close to $1.8\text{V}$.
    S4: $V_{avg} = 1.51\text{V}$.
    S3: $V_{max} = 5.72\text{V}$.
    The primary problem in S4 is the low excitation. SSHI should help there.

    Let's propose:
    - Proposal 1: `fbr_zener` (FBR + Zener clamp). This is the simplest way to fix S3.
    - Proposal 2: `sshi_fbr_zener` (SSHI + FBR + Zener clamp). This attempts to fix S2, S3, and S4.
    - Proposal 3: `sshi_half_zener` (A more efficient half-bridge SSHI, grounding $pzn$).

    Actually, for the half-bridge:
    - $pzn$ to $0$ (via a resistor or direct? The test bench adds a 1GOhm resistor, but we can just connect $pzn$ to $0$ with a $1\Omega$ resistor or just a component).
    - $L1$ from $pzp$ to $n1$.
    - $S1$ from $n1$ to $0$.
    - $D1$ from $pzp$ to $out$.
    - $D2$ from $0$ to $pzp$.
    - $D_z$ from $0$ to $out$.
    - $C_{out}$ from $out$ to $0$.
    - This might be more efficient because it uses fewer diodes.

    Let's double check the "half-bridge" piezo. If we ground $pzn$, we only get half the voltage amplitude. $\pm 3.2\text{V}$ becomes $0$ to $3.2\text{V}$? No, the piezo is a current source $I_p \sin(\omega t)$ in parallel with $C_p$. If $pzn$ is grounded, $pzp$ will swing $\pm 3.2\text{V}$. The full bridge uses both polarities. The half-bridge (with $pzn$ grounded) also uses both polarities of $pzp$ relative to $0$.

    Wait, the full bridge is:
    $D_1[pzp, out], D_2[pzn, out], D_3[0, pzp], D_4[0, pzn]$.
    This is effectively the same as grounding the "middle" of the bridge.

    Let's stick to the most robust ones.

    *Topology 1: FBR + Zener*
    - Components: D1, D2, D3, D4 (DSCH), Dz (DZ33), Cout (C).
    - Nodes: pzp, pzn, out, 0.

    *Topology 2: SSHI + FBR + Zener*
    - Components: L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn], G1 (SYNC), D1-D4 (DSCH), Dz (DZ33), Cout (C).

    *Topology 3: SSHI + Half-Bridge + Zener*
    - Components: L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, 0], G1 (SYNC), R_gnd [pzn, 0] (to ground pzn), D1 [pzp, out], D2 [0, pzp], Dz [0, out], Cout [out, 0].
    - Wait, $R_{gnd}$ can be a very small resistor. Let's use $1\Omega$.

    Let's refine Topology 2 (SSHI_FBR_Zener) components:
    - D1: [pzp, out], DSCH
    - D2: [pzn, out], DSCH
    - D3: [0, pzp], DSCH
    - D4: [0, pzn], DSCH
    - Dz: [0, out], DZ33
    - C1: [out, 0], 2.2uF (start value)
    - L1: [pzp, n1], 1mH (start value)
    - S1: [n1, pzn], G1
    - G1: SYNC, ton=0.5ms, phase=0, edges="both"

    Wait, in SSHI, the switch $S$ is usually used to flip the capacitor voltage $V_{Cp}$ at the peak. The current $I_p$ is a sine. The voltage $V_{Cp}$ is a cosine. The peaks of $V_{Cp}$ are at the zero crossings of $I_p$. The SYNC controller closes at the zero crossings of the current. This is exactly what's needed for SSHI.

    Let's check the component count for SSHI_FBR_Zener:
    D1, D2, D3, D4, Dz, C1, L1, S1, G1 = 9 components. Well within the 16 limit.

    Let's reconsider Topology 3 (Half-Bridge SSHI). Is it better?
    The full bridge is generally better for a floating source. If I ground $pzn$, I'm essentially forcing $pzn=0$. This is like a half-bridge.
    Let's try:
    1. FBR + Zener
    2. SSHI + FBR + Zener
    3. A variation of SSHI where the inductor is in a different place? No, let's try a "Parallel-SSHI" or "Synchronous Charge Extraction" if possible.
    Actually, a simple "Boost" style synchronous harvester:
    S1 [pzp, n1], L1 [n1, 0], S2 [n1, out], G1, G2.
    But that's more complex.

    Let's stick to:
    - `fbr_zener`
    - `sshi_fbr_zener`
    - `sshi_half_zener` (where $pzn$ is tied to $0$)

    Wait, for `sshi_half_zener`:
    - R1: [pzn, 0], 1 Ohm
    - L1: [pzp, n1], 1mH
    - S1: [n1, 0], G1
    - D1: [pzp, out], DSCH
    - D2: [0, pzp], DSCH
    - Dz: [0, out], DZ33
    - C1: [out, 0], 2.2uF
    - G1: SYNC, ton=0.5ms, edges="both", phase=0

    Actually, let's make Proposal 3 a "Symmetric SSHI" or something else.
    How about a "Voltage Doubler" style?
    Piezo $\to$ Half-wave $\to$ Storage $\to$ Half-wave $\to$ Storage.
    No, that's too many diodes.

    Let's try:
    1. `fbr_zener`: Basic bridge + Zener. (Fixes S3).
    2. `sshi_fbr_zener`: SSHI flipping + Bridge + Zener. (Fixes S2, S3, S4).
    3. `sshi_half_zener`: Grounded $pzn$ + SSHI + Half-bridge + Zener. (More efficient than FBR).

    Wait, one more thing: The `ton` for SSHI.
    The optimal $t_{on}$ is $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
    If $C_p = 25\text{nF}$ and $L = 1\text{mH}$, $t_{on} = 3.14 \times \sqrt{2.5 \times 10^{-8}} \approx 496 \mu\text{s}$.
    If $L = 10\text{mH}$, $t_{on} = 1.57 \text{ms}$ (too long, limit is $1\text{ms}$).
    If $L = 4.7\text{mH}$, $t_{on} = 1.07 \text{ms}$ (still slightly over).
    So $L$ will be around $1-4\text{mH}$.

    Let's refine the proposals:

    Proposal 1: `fbr_zener`
    - D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn], Dz [0, out], C1 [out, 0]
    - All DSCH except Dz (DZ33)

    Proposal 2: `sshi_fbr_zener`
    - L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn], G1, D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn], Dz [0, out], C1 [out, 0]
    - G1: ton=5e-4, edges="both", phase=0

    Proposal 3: `sshi_half_zener`
    - R1 [pzn, 0], 1 Ohm, L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, 0], G1, D1 [pzp, out], D2 [0, pzp], Dz [0, out], C1 [out, 0]
    - G1: ton=5e-4, edges="both", phase=0

    Actually, I'll use `L1` as a capacitor in some cases? No, SSHI needs an inductor.
    Is there any other topology?
    The "Cold Start" issue: $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$.
    FBR $t_{up}$ for S1 was $0.269\text{s}$.
    For S2, it never reached $1.8\text{V}$.
    For S4, it never reached $1.8\text{V}$.
    SSHI increases the energy extracted per cycle, so it should speed up $t_{up}$ and increase $V_{avg}$.

    One final check on SSHI:
    Does the switch $S$ need to be in parallel with the piezo or in series?
    In the standard SSHI:
    The inductor $L$ and switch $S$ are in parallel with the piezo.
    When $S$ closes, $C_p$ and $L$ form a resonant circuit, flipping $V_{Cp}$.
    So $L$ and $S$ should be connected across $pzp$ and $pzn$.
    My proposal: $L$ from $pzp$ to $n1$, $S$ from $n1$ to $pzn$. This is a series $L-S$ combination in parallel with $pzp-pzn$. Correct.

    Let's double check the diode directions for the full bridge:
    - $D_1$: $pzp \to out$
    - $D_2$: $pzn \to out$
    - $D_3$: $0 \to pzp$
    - $D_4$: $0 \to pzn$
    When $pzp$ is high and $pzn$ is low: $pzp \to D_1 \to out \to R_L \to 0 \to D_3 \to pzp$.
    When $pzp$ is low and $pzn$ is high: $pzn \to D_2 \to out \to R_L \to 0 \to D_4 \to pzn$.
    Correct.

    Let's double check the Zener:
    - $D_z$: $0 \to out$ (cathode on out).
    - When $V_{out} > 3.3\text{V}$, $D_z$ conducts. Correct.

    Wait, for the half-bridge:
    - $pzn$ is grounded.
    - $pzp$ swings $\pm 3.2\text{V}$.
    - $D_1$: $pzp \to out$.
    - $D_2$: $0 \to pzp$.
    - This is just a half-wave rectifier? No, $D_2$ is not helping to charge $out$.
    To get both halves, you need a full bridge or a charge pump.
    If $pzn$ is grounded, you only get energy when $pzp > V_{out}$.
    To get the other half, you'd need another stage.
    So the full bridge is better.

    Let's replace `sshi_half_zener` with another variation, maybe one that uses a different $t_{on}$ or phase? No, the optimizer does that.
    How about a "synchronous rectifier" using switches instead of diodes?
    But we only have 4 switches and 2 SYNCs.
    A full synchronous bridge needs 4 switches and 2 SYNCs (one for each pair).
    - S1, S2 (top pair)
    - S3, S4 (bottom pair)
    But $S1, S2$ would need to be timed perfectly.
    Actually, let's try a "SSHI with a larger storage capacitor" or "SSHI with a different inductor placement".
    No, let's try a "Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction (SECE)" simplified.
    SECE:
    1. $C_p$ charges.
    2. $S_1$ closes, $C_p$ dumps charge into $L$.
    3. $S_2$ closes, $L$ dumps charge into $C_{out}$.
    This needs 2 switches and 2 SYNCs.
    - S1: [pzp, n1], G1
    - L1: [n1, n2]
    - S2: [n2, out], G2
    But $G1$ and $G2$ would need to be phased.
    $G1$ at peak, $G2$ slightly after.
    Wait, the SYNC controller's `phase` is relative to the *excitation period*.
    The excitation is $100\text{Hz}$ ($T = 10\text{ms}$).
    A phase shift of $0.05$ is $0.5\text{ms}$.
    This could work!

    Let's try this for Proposal 3:
    - S1: [pzp, n1], G1 (ton=0.5ms, phase=0, edges="both")
    - L1: [n1, n2], 1mH
    - S2: [n2, out], G2 (ton=0.5ms, phase=0.05, edges="both")
